newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam launches blitz to improve railway safety.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam launches blitz to improve railway safety.

text.p: More than one thousand police and local officials gathered in central Hanoi on Monday to mark the start of a drive to improve safety on the country's treacherous railroads.

Police officers, many flying red flags from their jeeps and announcing the new campaign on loudspeakers, then sped through the capital to shops and houses beside the railway line where they ordered walls and sections of buildings to be knocked down.

The scene was reminiscent of last year's blitz on houses that were considered too near Hanoi's Red River dyke. Villas and makeshift houses beside the dyke were sliced down the middle, leaving rooms open to the elements, or demolished altogether.
In one area of Hanoi where dozens of tumbledown houses stand just two or three metres (6.5 to 9.8 feet) from the railway track, residents were told that they would have to move out.
However, a group of residents told Reuters that local authorities would first work out a compensation package and find them new homes before knocking the houses down.
The public pays little attention to railway lines in Vietnam. Many tracks double as makeshift marketplaces and short-cuts for pedestrians and cyclists, often with tragic consequences.
Last month a man, his pregnant wife and a child were killed by a train while crossing a railway line on a motorbike.
Official newspapers said the railroad campaign was launched simultaneously with a drive to clean up rivers and canals, and clear them of unauthorised obstructions and bridges.
The Lao Dong newspaper said that an order had been issued to pull down 600 canal-side houses in the northern port town of Haiphong because they violated safety regulations.
